204.title: Pauri 25, meaning: even hunger is a gift
204.hook: His generosity cannot be written; even pain and hunger are counted among His gifts (Japji 25)
204.howItsDone: Pauri 25 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs speak of accepting the bhaana, the divine will, in hard times, while also serving in the langar to feed the hungry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 25. Your line was bahutaa karam: generosity too great to write down. Did you give one thing without keeping score? Today, the hardest line in the stanza. Day two hundred four.

Ask someone about the worst year of their life, and then ask what came out of it. Sometimes there's a pause, and then something surprising. That's when I learned who my real friends were. That's when I stopped drinking. That's when I found out I could survive. Nobody chooses a year like that. Some still wouldn't give back what it taught them. Pauri 25 says something about hard things that is easy to misunderstand, so let's go slowly.
screen: `THE WORST YEAR OF YOUR LIFE.` → `WHAT CAME OUT OF IT?` → `GO SLOWLY HERE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is daat: a gift, something given. Pauri 25 began: His generosity is so great it can't be written. Then it looks at everyone receiving, in paraphrase. Many great warriors come begging at the Giver's door. Countless others, beyond counting. Some waste away in their own vices. Some take and take, then deny they ever received. Some fools just keep on eating. And then the line: so many endure pain, hunger and constant blows. In the original: eh bhi daat teree daataar. Even these are Your gifts, O Giver. Now, what does that mean, and what doesn't it mean? It doesn't mean hunger is fine, or that the hungry deserve it. Sikh life answers hunger by feeding people; that's what yesterday's langar is for. It doesn't tell anyone in pain to be quiet. What it says is that even the hard things come from the same hand, under the same Hukam, and can carry something in them. Guru Nanak says it elsewhere, in the Asa di Vaar, in paraphrase: pain can be the medicine, and comfort the sickness. The stanza goes on: release from bondage comes by the divine will; no one else has a say. The Giver knows, and the Giver gives. And the last lines: the one who is blessed to sing praise, Nanak says, is the king of kings. So the stanza ends not on wealth or even comfort, but on the gift of praise, which can come even in a hard year.
screen: `DAAT — A GIFT.` · `EH BHI DAAT TEREE DAATAAR.` · `NOT: HUNGER IS FINE.` · `PAIN AS MEDICINE.` · then, large: `EVEN THIS IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one difficulty, not the heaviest thing you carry, just something hard in your life right now. Hold it gently. Don't pretend it's good. Then ask quietly: is there anything inside this, something it's teaching me, someone it's brought closer, a strength it's showing? If you find one small thing, rest with it. If you don't, that's all right too; just breathe with the difficulty. The bell holds the time.
Daat. A gift. Pauri 25 counts even pain and hunger among the Giver's gifts, and ends on the gift of praise.
Your line: even this is a gift. Today, when something small goes wrong, ask once whether anything is hidden in it, and don't force an answer. Day two hundred four.

205.title: Pauri 26, sound: amul gun
205.howItsDone: Pauri 26 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs, for whom honest work, kirat karni, is one of the three pillars of daily life, hear its market words with special closeness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daat, the gift, even in hard things. Your line was even this is a gift. Did anything small that went wrong hide something? Today, Japji walks into a marketplace. Day two hundred five.

Picture an old bazaar in Punjab. Spice sellers calling out. Cloth merchants unrolling silk. A man with brass scales weighing lentils, a woman haggling over the price of mangoes. Everything has a price, and everybody's arguing about it. Guru Nanak knew this world well; tradition says he worked for a time as a storekeeper, weighing out grain. So when Pauri 26 begins, it borrows the language of the market: traders, trade, storehouses, scales. And then it breaks every price tag.
screen: `AN OLD PUNJAB BAZAAR.` → `EVERYTHING HAS A PRICE.` → `PAURI 26 BREAKS THE TAGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 26, in the original: amul gun amul vaapaar. Four words. Amul, a-MOOL: without price, priceless. Built like asankh, countless: a, not, plus mul, price. We'll open amul fully tomorrow. Gun, said with the u of put, not like the English word: virtues, qualities. The good things in a person, or in God. Vaapaar, vaa-PAAR: trade, business, dealing. The same word Punjabis still use for running a shop. So: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade. Then the stanza keeps going, in paraphrase: priceless the traders, priceless the storehouses. Priceless those who come to deal, priceless what they take away. And on it goes: priceless the scales, priceless the weights. Every piece of the market, one after another, is stamped amul. Hear the drumbeat of it. Amul gun, amul vaapaar: the same word striking at the start of each half, the way asankh did three weeks ago. Say it quickly and it sounds like a merchant calling out his wares; say it slowly and it sounds like a prayer. The point of borrowing the market isn't to despise it. Sikhs are known for honest work, kirat karni, and many are shopkeepers and traders. It's to say that when it comes to the virtues of the One, and the dealing between the soul and God, the scale has no numbers on it. Today, just the sound. Amul gun.
screen: `AMUL — WITHOUT PRICE.` · `GUN — VIRTUES, QUALITIES.` · `VAAPAAR — TRADE, DEALING.` · `EVERY PART OF THE MARKET.` · then, large: `AMUL GUN.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: amul gun, amul vaapaar. Once like a merchant calling out, brisk and clear. Then slowly, like a prayer. Then once more, as a whisper. Then sit, and let one good quality in someone you love come to mind: their patience, their humor, their kindness. Don't put a price on it. Just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 26. It opens amul gun, amul vaapaar: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade, and every part of the market after them.
Your line: amul gun. Today, next time you pay for something, let the line play, and think of one good thing in your life that has no price. Day two hundred five.

206.title: Pauri 26, meaning: priceless
206.hook: priceless His virtues and His dealings; many have described Him and gone on describing (Japji 26)
206.howItsDone: Pauri 26 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs hear its long list of describers, from the Vedas to the gods and sages, as a reminder that no one can fully tell the worth of the One.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 26. Your line was amul gun: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade. Did you find one thing in your life with no price? Today, the word amul itself. Day two hundred six.

Ask what someone would carry out of a burning house, and it's rarely the TV. It's the photo of a grandfather, a child's first shoes, a cheap ring that belonged to someone. Put any of those up for sale online and they're worth almost nothing. Try to take them away and they're worth everything. The price tag and the value have nothing to do with each other. Pauri 26 takes that feeling and applies it to everything, and then asks who could ever describe it.
screen: `OUT OF A BURNING HOUSE.` → `WORTHLESS TO SELL.` → `PRICELESS TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Amul: a, not; mul, price. Priceless. Not expensive, which still has a number. Beyond numbers altogether. Pauri 26 stamps it on everything. In paraphrase: priceless the virtues and the trade, the traders and the storehouses. Priceless those who come, priceless what they carry away. Priceless the love, and priceless those absorbed in it. Priceless the law and the court, the scales and the weights, the blessings and the signs of grace, the command itself. And then, in the original: amulo amul aakhiaa na jaae. Priceless beyond priceless, it can't be told. Then comes a long, wide turn. Many describe it, the stanza says, in paraphrase. The Vedas and the Puranas describe it; the learned describe it and give their commentaries. Brahmas describe it, Indras describe it. The gopis and Govind describe it. Shiva describes it, the siddhas describe it. Gods and demons, humans, sages and servants. So many have described it and gone on describing, have spoken and risen and left. If as many again were made, they still couldn't tell it. Notice who's in that list: scriptures, gods and sages from the world Guru Nanak lived in. None of them is mocked. All of them are honored as describers, and all of them fall short, because the thing is amul. It's as great as it wishes to be, and only the True One knows. So the stanza's lesson reaches all the way down to a pair of child's shoes. The most valuable things don't have a price. They're not less real for that. They're more.
screen: `AMUL — BEYOND ANY NUMBER.` · `AMULO AMUL AAKHIAA NA JAAE.` · `VEDAS, GODS, SAGES DESCRIBE.` · `ALL FALL SHORT; NONE MOCKED.` · then, large: `PRICELESS, ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing near you: a cup, your own hand, the chair, the light through the window. Look at it as if it were priceless, as if it couldn't be replaced. Notice its shape, its color, what it does for you, who made it, how long it has served. Let it be amul for these two minutes. Then close your eyes and rest. The bell holds the time.
Amul. Priceless: a, not, and mul, price. Pauri 26 says it of every virtue and every dealing, and says no describer, however great, can tell it all.
Your line: priceless, all of it. Today, treat one ordinary thing, a meal, a conversation, a walk, as if it couldn't be bought or replaced. Day two hundred six.

207.title: Pauri 27, sound: so dar kehaa
207.hook: so dar kehaa so ghar kehaa
207.tomorrow: Pauri 27, meaning: the house where all sing
207.howItsDone: Pauri 27 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib, and a version of the same stanza opens Rehras Sahib, the Sikh evening prayer, where the section is known as So Dar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amul, priceless. Your line was priceless, all of it. Did one ordinary thing get treated as if it couldn't be replaced? Today, a question asked at a door. Day two hundred seven.

Every building has a door most people never get to open. The principal's office. The kitchen behind a busy restaurant. Backstage at a concert. A kid can stand outside one and wonder what goes on in there, where the thing everyone depends on actually happens. Pauri 27 opens with a question like that, full of wonder: what is that door? What is that house? And Sikh prayer comes back to this question twice in a day: once in the morning in Japji, and again, in a version of its own, in the evening.
screen: `A DOOR MOST PEOPLE NEVER OPEN.` → `WHERE IT ALL HAPPENS.` → `WHAT IS THAT DOOR?`

segments.voice: Here's the first line in the original: so dar kehaa so ghar kehaa jit bahi sarab samaale. Let's take it apart. So: that. Dar, DUR: door, gate, and by extension a court, the place where a ruler hears people. Kehaa, KAY-haa: what kind of, what is it like. So dar kehaa: what is that door like? Then so ghar kehaa: ghar, GHUR, is house, home. What is that house like? Then: jit bahi, where You sit. Sarab samaale: caring for all, looking after everything. What is that door, what is that house, where You sit and care for all? Hear the balance: so dar kehaa, so ghar kehaa, two matching halves, then the line opens out into jit bahi sarab samaale, like a door swinging wide. After twenty-six stanzas of countless and priceless and no end, this one simply asks. It doesn't claim to know. It wonders. And this stanza lives a second life. Its words, with small differences, also appear later in the Guru Granth Sahib and open the evening prayer, Rehras Sahib, where that section is called So Dar, after these very first words. So the same question can be heard at dawn and again at dusk. Tomorrow we'll step through the door and hear who's singing inside. Today, just the question, and its sound. So dar kehaa.
screen: `DAR — DOOR. GHAR — HOUSE.` · `KEHAA — WHAT IS IT LIKE?` · `JIT BAHI SARAB SAMAALE.` · `SAID AT DAWN AND AT DUSK.` · then, large: `SO DAR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: so dar kehaa, so ghar kehaa, jit bahi sarab samaale. Slowly, feeling the two matching halves and then the opening. Say it twice more. Then sit quietly, and let it stay a question. Don't answer it. Just wonder: what is that door like, where all are cared for? Let the wondering be the practice. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 27. It opens so dar kehaa, so ghar kehaa: what is that door, what is that house, where You sit and care for all?
Your line: so dar. Today, each time you walk through a door, let the question come with you: what is that door like? Day two hundred seven.

screen: `DAY 207 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 27, MEANING: THE HOUSE WHERE ALL SING.`

208.title: Pauri 27, meaning: the house where all sing
208.hook: what is that door where you sit and care for all? Wind, water, fire and countless beings sing there (Japji 27)
208.howItsDone: Pauri 27 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib, and a version of it is sung in the evening as So Dar in Rehras Sahib; in gurdwaras, kirtan, sung praise with instruments, echoes its picture of the whole creation singing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the question at the door. Your line was so dar: what is that door, what is that house? Did a doorway bring the question with it? Today, we listen in. Day two hundred eight.

Sit outside at dawn some morning and just listen. First it seems quiet. Then you notice the birds, dozens of them, each with its own tune. Wind moving through a tree. Water somewhere, a gutter, a sprinkler. A far-off truck, a dog, a door. After a few minutes it doesn't sound like noise anymore. It sounds like an orchestra tuning up. Pauri 27 asked what that door is like, where the One sits and cares for all. Its answer isn't a description of a building. It's a sound.
screen: `OUTSIDE AT DAWN.` → `BIRDS, WIND, WATER, A DOG.` → `AN ORCHESTRA TUNING UP.`

segments.voice: What is that door, that house, where You sit and care for all? Pauri 27 answers with music, in paraphrase. There, countless instruments play, and countless are the players. So many ragas, the melodies of Indian music, and so many singers. Then who's singing? The elements first. In the original: gaavahi tuhano paun paanee baisantar. Wind, water and fire sing to You. Then, in paraphrase: the king of dharma sings at Your door, and the recorders who write down every deed. Shiva, Brahma and the goddess sing. Indra sings, among the gods. The siddhas, the celibates, the truthful, the contented, the brave warriors sing. The pandits and the sages with their Vedas, age after age. The continents and worlds and universes sing. Those who please You sing, Your devotees, steeped in Your love. And so many others sing that I can't even think of them all, Nanak says. Look at that list. Wind and fire. Gods whose names Guru Nanak's hearers knew. Scholars and warriors. Whole worlds and universes. Every one of them is singing to the same One. Nobody is outside the choir. Then the stanza settles, in paraphrase: He is, He is, forever true, the true Master, true His Name. He is, and will be, and won't pass away. Whatever pleases Him, He does; no one can give Him orders. He is the King, the King of kings, and Nanak says: live within His will. So the door from yesterday opens onto a sound. And the list is wide enough that an ordinary morning could fit inside it.
screen: `COUNTLESS INSTRUMENTS AND PLAYERS.` · `WIND, WATER AND FIRE SING.` · `GODS, SAGES, WORLDS, DEVOTEES.` · `HE IS, HE IS, FOREVER TRUE.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING IS SINGING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to whatever is around you: traffic, a fan, your own breath, a voice in another room. Instead of sorting sounds into good and bad, try hearing all of them as singing, each one its own voice in the choir. The hum of the fridge. The breath in your nose. Let nothing be noise for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 27. At that door, countless instruments play; wind, water and fire, gods, sages and whole worlds sing. He is, forever true.
Your line: everything is singing. Today, when a sound annoys you, a horn, an alarm, a crying child, try once to hear it as one more voice in the choir. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: Pauri 28, sound: mundaa santokh
209.howItsDone: Pauri 28 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; pauris 28 to 31 are addressed to the yogis, and each ends with aades tisai aades, salutation to Him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the house where all sing. Your line was everything is singing. Did one annoying sound become part of the choir? Today, a new stretch of Japji, and some new people in it. Day two hundred nine.

Ash on the skin. Matted hair. A patched coat, a bag over the shoulder, and in each ear a heavy ring. In Guru Nanak's time, that outfit marked the Nath yogis, wandering ascetics who left home to master body and mind. You could tell who they were before they said a word. Tradition says Guru Nanak met and talked with yogis like these more than once on his travels. The next four stanzas of Japji speak to them, in their own language, using the very things they carried. Today, the first line, and its sound.
screen: `ASH, A COAT, RINGS IN THE EARS.` → `THE NATH YOGIS.` → `JAPJI SPEAKS TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 28 in the original: mundaa santokh saram pat jholee dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot. Let's take the words one by one. Mundaa, MOON-daa: earrings, the large rings of the yogi. Santokh, sun-TOKH: contentment. You know it; it was our word on day one hundred eighty, enough, by listening. Saram, SUH-rum: effort, or modesty; commentators read it both ways. Pat: honor, the word from Pauri 14, going forth with honor. Jholee, JHO-lee: the pouch or begging bag the yogi carries. Dhiaan: meditation, attention. Bibhoot, bi-BHOOT: the ashes the yogis smeared on their bodies. So the line is built from pieces of the yogi's outfit, earrings, bag, ashes, each one paired with an inner quality. We'll open what that pairing means tomorrow. Today, notice the craft. Guru Nanak doesn't argue with the yogis in abstract terms. He picks up the very objects they carry and speaks through them. And one more sound to listen for. Each of these four stanzas, 28 to 31, ends with the same words: aades tisai aades. Commentators explain that aades was the greeting the Nath yogis used with each other. So Guru Nanak even closes in their greeting, and turns it: salutation to Him, salutation to the One. Say the first two words and you have today's carry. Mundaa santokh. Earrings, contentment. The outfit, and what it could mean.
screen: `MUNDAA — THE YOGI'S EARRINGS.` · `SANTOKH, SARAM, PAT, DHIAAN.` · `THE OUTFIT, PIECE BY PIECE.` · `AADES — THE YOGIS' GREETING.` · then, large: `MUNDAA SANTOKH.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: mundaa santokh, saram pat jholee, dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot. Slowly, letting each piece land. Say it again, a little quieter. Then, a third time, only the first two words: mundaa santokh. Then sit, and let the word santokh, contentment, rest where earrings would rest, close to your ears, close to what you hear. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 28. It opens mundaa santokh: earrings of contentment, a bag of effort and honor, ashes of meditation. Guru Nanak speaks to the yogis in their own things.
Your line: mundaa santokh. Today, when you put on something you wear every day, a ring, a watch, earrings, let it remind you of contentment. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: Pauri 28, meaning: contentment for earrings
210.hook: make contentment your earrings, modesty your bowl, meditation your ashes; conquer the mind and you conquer the world (Japji 28)
210.howItsDone: Pauri 28 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs quote man jeetai jag jeet, conquer the mind and you conquer the world, as a summary of living a disciplined inner life within family and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 28. Your line was mundaa santokh: earrings, and contentment. Did something you wear remind you? Today, the end of a week, and what the whole outfit means. Day two hundred ten.

First, the week. Daat: even this is a gift. Amul gun, and priceless, all of it. So dar, the door. Everything is singing. And yesterday, mundaa santokh. Now think about uniforms. A nurse's scrubs, a judge's robe, a team jersey. Put one on and people know who you are. But everybody also knows the uniform isn't the job. A jersey doesn't make the shot. Scrubs don't make you kind. Pauri 28 talks to the yogis about their uniform, and it's gentle, and it's direct.
screen: `THE WEEK: GIFT, PRICELESS, THE DOOR.` → `SCRUBS, A ROBE, A JERSEY.` → `THE UNIFORM ISN'T THE JOB.`

segments.voice: Pauri 28 goes through the yogi's outfit piece by piece, and gives each one an inner meaning. In paraphrase: make contentment your earrings. Make effort and modesty your begging bag, and honor what you carry in it. Make meditation the ashes you smear on your body. Let the awareness of death be your patched coat. Keep your body pure, the way you'd keep a vow. Let faith be your walking staff, and a right way of living your discipline. Then a line that borrows the name of a yogi order and opens it wide. The Aaee Panth was one of the respected Nath sects. Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: let all people be your order, the whole of humanity your brotherhood. And then the line behind today's carry, in the original: man jeetai jag jeet. Conquer the mind, and you conquer the world. Every outer thing the yogi had set out to master, the body, hunger, the world, comes down to one inner thing: the mind. And the stanza closes: aades tisai aades, salutation to Him, salutation, the primal one, pure, without beginning, beyond harm, the same through every age. How do Sikhs hear this? Sikh tradition doesn't ask anyone to leave home for the forest. The Gurus lived as householders, with families and work. Many Sikhs hear Pauri 28 as saying the discipline the yogi wore on the outside can be carried on the inside, anywhere, in a kitchen or an office. The earrings become contentment. The ashes become meditation. And the whole world becomes your order.
screen: `EARRINGS OF CONTENTMENT.` · `MEDITATION FOR ASHES, FAITH A STAFF.` · `ALL PEOPLE YOUR ORDER.` · `MAN JEETAI JAG JEET.` · then, large: `CONQUER THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Choose one inner ornament to wear today: contentment, modesty, honor, faith, or the steadiness of meditation. Just one. Picture it as something you put on, the way you'd put on a ring or a coat. Where does it sit? How does it feel to carry? Breathe with it, and let it settle on you. If the mind wanders, notice it, and come back; that is the conquering, one return at a time. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 28. Contentment for earrings, meditation for ashes, faith for a staff, all people your order. Conquer the mind, and you conquer the world.
Your line: conquer the mind. Today, when your mind runs off toward a worry or a grudge, bring it back once, gently. That's one small victory. Day two hundred ten.

fork.setup: you're a yogi who has worked for years to master the world. what does Pauri 28 say is the real conquest?
fork.reveal: man jeetai jag jeet: conquer the mind, and you conquer the world.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 28: conquer the mind, and you conquer the world.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about earrings.
what it means: the yogi's outward discipline, carried inward: contentment, meditation, faith, and a mind brought under control.
what a scholar hears: Aaee Panth names a Nath sect, widened to all humanity; man jeetai jag jeet became one of the most quoted lines of Japji.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6 (Japji, Pauri 28, the outfit lines and aades tisai aades)
